profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting at a mid-sized quantitative investment firm evaluating a proposal to adapt a research paper's enhanced DQN trading approach into the firm's internal strategy prototyping framework. The context is that a research lead has circulated a design document describing a Phase 1 prototype for single-asset trading on BTC/USD and AAPL using CNN-based state encoders plus Double/Dueling DQN, prioritized replay, and noisy networks. The agenda is to review whether the proposal is 'ready for prototyping,' identify any missing implementation details that could block approval, and decide what changes are needed before the work is handed to the engineering pod. The expected outcome is a conditional approval of the design with a short list of revisions and a shared understanding of what the prototype package will include.

members.name: Lena Park
members.expertise: Reinforcement learning for portfolio strategies, experimental design, backtest interpretation
members.background: Former buy-side quant researcher with a PhD in machine learning; she now sponsors early-stage strategy research and reviews model designs before they move into the firm's prototyping queue.
members.private_state: She wants the design approved quickly so the team can claim progress for the quarterly research roadmap, but she also wants enough rigor that the prototype's results can later be shown to the investment committee without embarrassment.
hidden_assumptions: If a design is 'ready for prototyping,' it only needs enough detail for a research-grade implementation inside the sandbox, not full downstream integration details.
The 'baseline' in this proposal naturally means the firm's existing internal DQN benchmark configuration from last quarter, because that is the only comparison she cares about for approval.
When the document says 'transaction costs,' that implicitly refers to the firm's standard flat cost add-on used in research backtests, not venue-specific execution modeling.
A 'stable' result means the enhanced model behaves consistently across repeated seeds and adjacent time windows, even if it has not yet been stress-tested across full production-style market regimes.

members.name: Arjun Mehta
members.expertise: Model deployment pathways, data pipelines, reproducibility infrastructure, trading simulation systems
members.background: Previously led ML systems at an electronic trading vendor; he now reviews research designs to ensure they can be reproduced, instrumented, and transitioned into the firm's shared experimentation stack.
members.private_state: He wants to prevent a prototype from being approved in a way that later creates hidden engineering work, especially around replay data generation, environment compatibility, and auditability.
hidden_assumptions: If a design is 'ready for prototyping,' it should already specify enough operational detail that another engineer could reproduce the exact setup in the shared platform without informal handoffs.
The 'baseline' means the published vanilla DQN setup from the paper being extended, because otherwise the claimed uplift is not externally interpretable.
When a proposal includes 'transaction costs,' it should already encode the simulator's actual per-asset fee and slippage settings rather than a generic research placeholder.
A 'stable' result means performance remains acceptable under the platform's standard holdout slices, seed pack, and stress scenarios, since instability discovered later is expensive to unwind.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the design should be 'ready for prototyping' after review.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 believes this means the research logic, feature/state definition, and experiment plan are sufficiently clear for a quant researcher to build a sandbox version and iterate.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 believes this means the document already specifies enough reproducible implementation detail, interfaces, and environment assumptions for the shared platform team to execute it with minimal ambiguity.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In design reviews, 'ready for prototyping' sounds like a standard maturity gate, so both use the phrase confidently and cooperatively without spelling out the bar they have in mind.

misalignment_points.topic: Which baseline the uplift is measured against
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss beating 'the baseline' and keeping the comparison consistent.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 is referring to the firm's internal baseline DQN trader from last quarter, which uses the house observation schema and cost assumptions.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 is referring to the plain vanilla DQN configuration described in the academic study, because he assumes the proposal's purpose is to reproduce and extend that published benchmark.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: There is only one phrase—'the baseline'—and both assume the referent is obvious from context; each interpretation fits the discussion and does not immediately create contradiction.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as transaction costs in the prototype
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the prototype should include 'transaction costs' so results are realistic.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the firm's standard research penalty, a flat basis-point deduction per trade applied uniformly in backtests to avoid obviously inflated returns.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means explicit simulator settings for commission plus slippage by instrument and order size bucket, matching the platform's normal execution realism defaults.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Using transaction costs in trading reviews is routine, and both meanings are individually reasonable; because they agree realism matters, neither thinks to unpack the exact cost model.

misalignment_points.topic: What the review covers under the prototype package
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether 'the prototype package' includes the evaluation harness and handoff artifacts.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 assumes the package covers the model design, training loop, and summary evaluation notebook needed for internal research comparison.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 assumes the package also includes the standardized experiment config, replay-data generation job, seed manifest, and hooks into the shared evaluation harness.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Both talk about the prototype as a single deliverable, and the omitted items feel like obvious supporting materials from each person's vantage point, so the boundary mismatch stays implicit.

turns.inner_thought: I want to get this through the gate today if possible. For me, ready for prototyping means the research design is clear enough that one of the quants can build it in the sandbox and start learning from the first runs. I do not need every downstream platform detail nailed down yet, but I do need enough rigor that if the prototype works, I can defend the setup later.

turns.inner_thought: The design itself looks reasonable, but I need to avoid another handoff where research says it was approved and engineering later discovers half the operational assumptions were implicit. If it's ready for prototyping, another engineer should be able to run it in the shared stack without chasing the author for missing details. And the prototype package should include the surrounding reproducibility pieces, not just the model idea.
